message.content:
Lions (family *Felidae*, order Carnivora) and zebras (family *Equidae*, order Perissodactyla) are both members of the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**.  
Their most recent common ancestor was a small, early mammal that lived roughly **70–80 million years ago**, sometime during the Late Cretaceous/early Paleocene. This ancestor would have been a basal Laurasiatherian—an insect‑eating, semi‑arboreal mammal that gave rise to the diverse lineages that eventually became the carnivores, perissodactyls, cetartiodactyls, chiropterans, and others.  

In other words, lions and zebras share a common ancestor that existed in the same time frame as the earliest members of the Laurasiatherian superorder, long before the distinct families *Felidae* and *Equidae* evolved.
